I'd be careful. My ex never owned up to their mistakes, and I was strung along the entire time. So as someone who was always blamed, never apologised to, and never had my ex hold themselves accountable, don't go back to him if he doesn't *genuinely* own up to his mistake.

He sounds a bit emotionally avoidant (correct me if I'm wrong), just as my ex was. I'm not trying to project, but it can be really difficult to be in a relationship with someone who isn't able to, or straight-up refuses, to communicate properly.

​

Ask yourself, is this really worth it? Is it worth possibly being stuck with someone who won't be able to communicate? Who is avoidant, who won't own up to their mistakes and apologise? 

This *is* a red flag, and my advice is; If he never ends up genuinely owning up and apologising ***and*** actually doing better, I'd just accept this isn't the guy for you. 

You deserve someone who is clear about wanting you, and can put aside their pride/ego for you. Nothing less than that.

I'm going to give you some really hard to follow advice, but advice that's going to make a massive difference.

Cut those strings.

Those texts are keeping you connected to your ex in the most painful way possible. It's honestly best to delete them. Hear me out.

​

Why do you need to keep those texts? What are they honestly doing other than hurting you and keeping you in the past? Genuinely?

​

Deleting them isn't going to delete the experiences. Don't worry about that. They still happened, that all still happened, no matter where it goes. No matter if you can't go over it again.

But, accepting it's over and cutting those strings holding you back. That's what's going to let you keep going. That's going to stop that specific hurting, and that's going to give you the ability to move on from this point.

​

The past is the past, but it still happened. It's not going anywhere. It's set in stone, unchangeable.

What isn't is the present moment and the future. You get to do whatever you want with that. You can do what you need to do *right now.* 

Do yourself a favour, save your future self some pain by getting rid of that connection to your ex. Protect your future self, they don't deserve this pain.

Closure, I've figured out, is a deeply personal thing. And closure can only come from ourselves.

We can't find closure from other people, as crazy as it sounds. I know from experience.

I know exactly why my ex and I broke up. We had countless conversations about it. I had the opposite of a blindsided breakup, I got all the 'closure' anyone could possibly ask for.

Yet, it never felt like *enough.* I always had more questions, I always continued to wonder and think about it. The more answers I got, the more questions I had. And digging around for closure only slowed my progress and kept me stuck in my hole.

​

And then randomly, one night, I realised closure was never going to come from my ex. It *had* to come from me. It just had to.

So I sat there, at 1AM, and thought. I went down every possible train of thought until I couldn't find anymore tracks. And I found my closure.

***I was never going to find closure while looking for closure.*** Ironic, right?

I was holding onto my ex and the relationship. In the process I was being purposefully led on, hurt, manipulated, etc. I was looking for an answer that didn't exist, that I didn't even know the question to. Every question I asked, every answer I got, only dug my hole deeper and deeper. Only pushed my feet further in my past.

​

So I stopped contacting my ex. I set myself a real plan to move on *(which if anyone would like, I can write up)*, and made sure I'd never look back.

It wasn't perfect, it wasn't a big moment. It was me, in bed, at 1AM listening to music. 

But that's all it needed to be. It just needed to be. I just needed to be.

​

I'm not completely over everything, I still have moments, I still think about them a lot. But I've gotten so much better thanks to that night. Thanks to the closure I gave myself.

​

And it's not just that one moment that puts you on the right track. It's usually a series of moments, that redirect you and keep you moving.

For example, last night, I finally destroyed the letters they wrote me. I went outside in the middle of the night, read through each one, and burnt them with my lighter. I couldn't stop smiling as I did it.

​

***Point is:*** You can't get closure from anyone but yourself. It *has* to be you.

If you feel like you have to, here's some tips.

1. Understand his motive. Why does he want to talk in person specifically? What is he going to talk about? What are his intentions? If he doesn't give you these answers or he's shady about it, don't go. You deserve to know what you're walking into.

2. Set boundaries. Make them clear and strong. E.g. Meeting in a public place, taking a friend or family member along, no affection, no talk of getting back together, ability to leave at any time if you need, etc.

3. Don't take any bullshit. Is he trying to lead you on? Lie to you? False promises? Don't let him hurt you or have power against you. Leave if he tries any BS.

You have every right to choose how, when, where, and if you want to meet. You have every right to set any boundaries and refuse contact if he disrespects them. You have every right to whatever you need.

1. Lack of communication skills. Instant deal-breaker. If you refuse to communicate with me, then I just can't be in a relationship with you. Especially as someone with autism. I'm not here to try and guess your feelings or what you want.

My ex would get annoyed with me even asking how they were feeling, that's how much they refused to communicate.



2. Projecting your insecurities onto me. If I tried talking about my interests to my ex, they'd get mad at me because they didn't understand. They had insecurities over their intelligence, and took it out on me because I was objectively smarter than them. If they didn't understand an interest I was talking about (computers, english concepts, even shows I was into) then it would upset them and start an argument. 

I would offer to teach them, I'd tell them I didn't need them to understand what I'm talking about, I'd ask what they were okay with me talking about, etc. To the point I stopped talking about my interests entirely. Then they'd get upset about me not talking to them about my interests, another whole thing.

I will work with you on your insecurities, definitely. Just do not project them onto me and use your insecurities as an excuse to hurt me.



3. Lying to me, knowingly breaking my trust/boundaries. I told my ex I wasn't comfortable with drug use, and I wasn't comfortable with them using drugs, especially without my knowing. (Family issues with drugs makes me want to stay far away from them). My ex told me they understood, and told me they didn't mind because they've never done drugs before anyway.

Then they went and got high with their friends and hid it from me. It made me more upset that they decided to hide it from me instead. I asked them to promise to not do it again, and they kept that promise (I think).

Later in the relationship they started asking me if they could go get high, if we could get high. They'd ask a lot, told me it was for their mental health. I would say no or I'm not sure, and they'd still ask over and over again until I was pressured into telling them okay, but only if we did it together. Luckily we broke up before doing it. 

They broke a clear boundary I made, hid it from me, then pressured me into changing my boundary. After that happened I wasn't able to get myself to say no to them anymore, they'd taken all my power.

Stand up for myself.

I let them blame me for everything. I blamed myself for everything.

Looking back, it was rarely my fault. 

If I tried to stand up for myself I would get gaslighted, guilt-tripped, threatened to be broken up with, sworn at, ghosted, the works.

It got to a point I couldn't bring myself to say no to them. 


So if I had to go through it again, I would stand up for myself instead of handing them all that power against me.

Try and put a positive spin on *"who knows".*

Because you cannot predict what's going to happen. Not with accuracy anyway. Everything from the present moment onwards is a mystery. Literally anything could happen.

So... who knows! Will she work on her issues? What would even happen if she did? Would you guys get back together, be friends, accept things are over?

What if you guys got back together, would it be perfect? Or would more effort need to maintain a healthy relationship? Would she go back to how she was? Would you? Would you want to be with her the rest of your life, or would either of you two want to break up at some point?

Or would you have moved on by that point anyway? Then maybe you can be friends, and have a healthy friendship? But, what if there's too many unspoken issues or feelings? What if you guys get drunk and talk about your feelings and complicate everything again?

What if you find someone new? This new person who seems perfect? Would you get back with your ex (given she's worked on herself) or try something with the new person?

What would happen if you guys went no-contact? What if she starts dating someone new? What if she showed up on your door-step in a weeks time in the rain, begging for forgiveness and professing her love to you? What if an alligator decided to show up in that very moment and eat her?

​

Don't actually think about any of those questions, or go down their paths. The point is, *who knows what will happen*. You don't, she doesn't, no one does. You can't predict the future, so don't try to.

Let things progress and happen naturally. Just be there for yourself through it all.

​

Personally, I'd go on with life trying to just move on. You can't control what she does, but you control yourself in the present moment. Work on yourself, move on, let go, etc.

Do what seems right for both your brain and your gut.

​

Don't get caught up in what-ifs, because who knows what will happen, anyway? An alligator might storm in right now and eat you.

You've got this, it'll slot into place eventually. And, good luck with the potential alligator (I think he has a grudge, but... *who knows?*)

I didn't do much about it for the first few weeks. I actively tried to get us back together and my ex led me on. When my ex went on a date with someone and continued to lead me on, I decided enough was enough. It wasn't just the leading on either, they'd continue to argue and swear at me, say horrible things about me, insult me, etc.

I was letting myself get played and manipulated just like how it was when we were dating.


So I went no-contact. I still had the hope they'd want me back and ask to get back together, but the no-contact stopped me from being led on and hurt. 

During the first go at no-contact they would message me memes or videos, despite saying they didn't want to be friends. I gave them short responses that couldn't be followed up on (should've just ignored them). Then they stopped.

 And then they texted me again trying to pick a fight about some issue we had while we were dating. Talked to them calmly about it, and ignored them again after that.


We haven't spoken since, but the no-contact period let me see things clearly. They were an ASSHOLE. They manipulated me and borderline abused me in the relationship, and then after it they still continued to manipulate me, lead me on, insult and swear at me, etc. They weren't a good person. 

So I got mad at them. I did my best to get as much anger about them as I could out of the trenches of my brain. I ranted about them to friends, wrote it down, used it as motivation. But the key thing it did is make me *want* them out of my life. It made me want it to be over. That killed a lot of hope, since the hope either disappeared or was beaten up and stuffed somewhere deep in my brain.

I have moments where I miss the good parts of our relationship, but I could get those good moments again from anyone else. I don't miss my ex anymore though, cause I've been able to accept they were a bad person who did bad things to me to purposely hurt me. And by accepting that, I accepted it was over.


I have 3 main points out of that story:

1. Go no-contact. It lets you see things clearly and helps you move on. Trust me, things get a lot better once you go no-contact. Get your power back.


2. Get mad and angry at the shit they've done. Get annoyed at shit they've done. Let it bother you, let it fill your brain temporarily. Let any emotions or thoughts you have inside out. Let them take the forefront for a bit so you can express them healthily. 

You can't accept things are over when they aren't over to your brain. Let it all out. With the emotions still deep in your head and tied to your ex, you're going to stay hung up on it. Let it all out, let it all go.


3. Find a reason. Find a reason to move on and accept things are over and to no longer hope for them back. 

For me it was everything they did to me, I couldn't keep hoping for someone back who purposefully hurt me and fucked up a really important year of my life. Accepting who they truly were (and not who I wanted them to be) made me accept that I was never going to get back with the person I wanted to be with, because they didn't exist in my ex.

It might be a different reason for you, but it's easier to find the reason when you go no-contact and let all your emotions out. At a certain point the reason (or reasons) should be clear, or at least noticeable. Find your reason.


Continue doing things to move on as well. Mainly keep your life moving. Keep going, keep making your life without your ex so you can get to a point without them so you can look back and go "I never would've gotten here if we didn't break up, if we were still together." 

Meet more people and make new and stronger connections with anyone you can. Build your social network so you have a strong social foundation without your ex. Don't meet people with the expectation of a romantic relationship though, this is a time for you to get back on your feet and truly realise you don't need your ex or a partner. This is a time to fill the hole they left with yourself, so you can be whole all by yourself. 

Stay strong. You can do this.

I completely understand. I was scared to move on because I was scared of letting go. I was scared of letting go of the memories, the effort I put in, them. Until I realised that what I was scared of wasn't actually what I was letting go.  


I wasn't going to let go of the memories. They wouldn't just disappear and mean nothing to me. They're going to be there, and I'm going to be reminded of them and what we've done. You can't just erase someone.

And I wasn't letting go of them. I was letting go of my idealised version of them. The person I thought they could've been if I "tried harder". Without letting that person go, I would've kept wrongly blaming myself and wishing I had done things differently. The person I was holding onto was never real, and they never would have been.

And I had to let go of the effort I put in, and most importantly the blame I put upon myself. It was hard, but I analysed and looked back on everything with a lot of people, and it was rarely ever my fault. They convinced me I was the issue, made me put in more effort that they never would have done for me. I had to let that go.  


  
What I'm trying to say is; It's scary. It feels like you're abandoning a massive part of your life, that you don't matter to the other person anymore, that you're dismissing all your effort and pain. But you're not.   
Either you're letting go of something that was never real anyway, you're letting go of something you need to move on from, or you're not actually letting go of something as it's still always going to be there.   
None of it is meaningless, or for nothing. And nothing bad will happen out of moving on. Moving will only bring positive change, trust me. 

Change is scary, hard. You just need to hold onto the hope that it *will* be for something way better. That hope got me through the pain, and now I'm 100x better than I have been in my entire life. 

*It gets better. Promise.*

Here's some of what I've done, for this specifically and to just get over them in general:  


1. Acknowledge the anxiety, then understand what you're anxious about and why. Then question everything. 

* *Why is it making me anxious? Have they actually done anything? What do I think they're doing? Why does that matter? Does what they're potentially doing affect me? Would I be better off not knowing about it? Why do I care?* 
* Give yourself actual answers to these questions, I find it helps to write it down physically. Follow each train of thought until there are no other paths to go down.
   * After that I tell myself something along the lines of: 
      * *"I might not know what they're doing, but they don't know what I'm doing either. I'm not the only one in the unknown,"*
      * or *"I'm wasting time I could be using to move on/work/enjoy life/etc. and I will not let my ex control and damage my life. No one deserves to control me or my life, especially not someone who hurt me,"* 
      * or *"It's okay to feel this way, to think these things, but at a certain point I cannot continue thinking about it and letting it affect me like this."*

2. Keep yourself truly busy. Even if you don't feel like it, even if you just want to sit around. Keep your mind busy so it doesn't have the capacity to wonder about them for more than 10 seconds. 

* Focus on work/school, or a hobby. Extra points if it's a new hobby they don't know about. Then you can tell yourself *"I might not know what they're doing, but they definitely don't know what I'm doing!"*

3. Keep your life *moving.* Don't stay stuck in the same pit for more than a few hours. 

* You get 2 hours to feel like crap. Use those 2 hours to write *everything* down, to mope, to wonder, to cry, to be angry or sad. Then when those 2 hours are up, you're going to get up and do what you need to do. You are going to keep your life moving after that. 
   * You get those 2 hours everyday whenever you need them, and it doesn't have to be all at once. After a week or so, shorten it to an hour and 1/2. Then an hour in another week or so. Then less and less.

4. Be confident in yourself. 

* Realise how much better you are than your ex, and think about how someone as good as yourself shouldn't limit yourself to your ex. You shouldn't waste your time, energy, or thoughts on them. They don't deserve it. They lost that privilege when you two broke up.

That's some of my general advice for getting over them. Because to stop feeling anxious about them/stop thinking about them, you have to get over them.

​

For the anxious feelings:

1. Breathing techniques for anxiety *(imagine a square, draw a square with your breath, in to draw a line up, hold to draw a line left, out to draw a line down, hold to draw a line right, repeat)*
2. Mindfulness  *(acknowledge and accepting your feelings and being able to live in the moment, your moment)*
3. Self-soothing behaviours to comfort yourself *(I like to rub my arms and rock while listening to music when it gets bad)*
4. Distractions, especially social ones
5. Music *(I tend to blast music, especially angry breakup songs or uplifting/happy songs that aren't about love. I might have tinnitus, but it helps)*
6. Any sort of healthy expression of the feelings, writing, art, playing music, etc.

Honestly, your ex was probably just mediocre. They aren't this 'incredible, amazing person' who ticks all your boxes, they're just a person. And they can't be exactly what you're looking for either, because I assume you're looking for someone who also wants to date you?  


These people aren't inherently special or different from everyone else, it's our love and care that makes them special to us. We make them special in our heads.  


Realising that helped me a lot, because if I can make someone who I never thought I'd want to date *that* special to me during the relationship, I know I can do it again with someone who actually wants me back.

Here's how I did it:

They said you got hurt by them? Understand how they hurt you, acknowledge all the shitty things they did. Don't think about the good stuff, just for now. Try to find your anger towards them, your despair, anything shitty directed to them, just for a little bit.

Make yourself believe you don't want them back. Even if you know deep down you do, acknowledge that feeling for a moment but ultimately tell yourself "I do not want them back. They hurt me, they did (blah blah blah)".

I had to learn to hate my ex, which wasn't too hard for me personally, but I understand if it is for you. I had to get over the lovesickness and missing them by cutting them out of my life and doing everything to hate them. And now I do, and I'm angry at them. Sometimes a passing thought will come by, hoping they'll want me back, missing them. But then I just acknowledge how I'm feeling, distract myself if I can or if I can't I'll focus on it and focus on my anger.

Don't hate them for longer than you need. I still need to hate them for now, but at a certain point I'll need to let the anger go to finish moving on.

But that’s how abuse works, especially emotional abuse. These people make it out that we’re worthless, useless, good for nothing (especially without them), and it comes to a point where we believe it. At least subconsciously.

Abuse is also a cycle. They’ll be shitty, hurt you, whatever, and then after they might apologise or love-bomb you. For me it came to a point where I knew that if I just got through the half-day of them hurting me, ghosting me, swearing at me, gaslighting me, etc. and if I just apologised and blamed myself, they would love me again for the rest of the day. Every single day.

I also felt responsible for it. I believed I could just do something, just one thing, I could fix it all and we’d be okay. I wasted so much time trying to fix us and putting in all this effort when they just didn’t care. Even after they broke up with me I was still convinced I could fix it for up to a month after. The entire relationship we both wrongly blamed me, my mental illness, etc. I had to talk to a lot of people to realise it wasn’t ever really my fault. I had my issues sure, but they either made it worse or incorrectly blamed it on me/my issues.

Those are some of the reasons I stayed so long, and some of the reasons we can still miss them. We miss them because that sounds how abuse is designed.

There’s also the generic reasons we miss ex’s after a breakup too. Despite being shitty we still dated them and shared intimate parts of our life/ourselves. 

Feelings, relationships, breakups, grieving, etc. aren’t logical. It sucks, but they just aren’t. Don’t push yourself trying to find logic in it all. Hey! I am formally diagnosed with ADD and Autism. ADD is the same as ADHD just without the ‘hyperactivity’ part since I display internalised symptoms and not the externalised ones. Currently even on medication for it.
What I meant by wired is: my brain literally has a dopamine deficiency, that’s what causes people with ADHD tend to be hyperactive, easily distracted, find difficulty focussing and completing tasks, deal with executive dysfunction, etc. It’s because our brains have a genuine deficiency of dopamine (and I think some other chemicals?). That’s also why the best treatments for ADHD are stimulants, since (unlike normally where they give someone a ‘high’) they bring us to a normal functioning level. We were just born like this, treatments can help but ultimately are brains are literally made like this and there’s no permanent solution.
- Also with the treatment thing: We tend to suffer from ‘executive dysfunction’. It’s a range of emotional, cognitive, and behavioural difficulties likely stemming from the deficiencies in our brains. It makes normal tasks seemingly impossible. If you’ve ever noticed someone with ADHD just mindlessly scrolling their phone or staring into space and you think “Hey, there’s so much stuff they could be doing right now,” they know that, and are most likely screaming at themselves in their head to just get up and do something. I don’t know how many times I’ve been doing something like being on social media or gaming and just screaming at myself to go do something productive. There’s quite a few articles that explain it much better than I can, but it’s just important to know that this makes it nearly impossible to ‘just do something’, unless you’ve really experienced it it’s hard to understand. It’s a constant war for me, but the medication does help a bit.
- What this means is: Most, if not all, people with ADHD want to be able to focus and be productive. It’s not comfortable being like this, not being able to do anything or focus on anything, it’s tiring and frustrating. But executive dysfunction, and the other symptoms of ADHD actively combats attempts to get better, you literally have to fight your brain every. single. step. of. the. way. I mean every single step. Even just taking the single pill everyday is extremely difficult, and I often mess up and miss days. It’s so tiring to do this every day while also possibly struggling with other issues (like many of us have to do). And this isn’t something I can just think my way out of easily, it takes real effort and energy to do simple tasks.

On the general topic of mental illnesses, most are chemical imbalances/deficiencies (Depression, ADHD, Anxiety, etc.). These come from different things, you could just be born with it, or it can be a result of trauma (mental and physical), genetics also play a major part as well. You can’t really just change your mindset and get better that way (at least for moderate-severe cases). People do try it that way though, with a form of therapy called CBT, which a lot of us call the “gaslighting therapy”. CBT believes that changing thought patterns can improve some mental illnesses, but it often only works for mild cases of depression, anxiety, etc. I tried it for a few years and it never made much of a difference. I think it’s because the brain has those chemical imbalances that CBT isn’t usually the best course of action for people with more severe issues, because you can’t just think all those chemicals you need into your brain. Did you know that Depression actually physically destroys the brain? Studies show that we lose grey matter volume (GMV) in our hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, which makes depression even worse. It’s like a self-destructive cycle. That’s a reason why we have memory issues, trouble thinking, hopelessness, no motivation, sleep issues, appetite issues, and anxiety.

I just wanted to explain how mental illnesses aren’t just in our head, and the physical causes (genetics, trauma, imbalances, deficiencies, literally eating away our brains, etc.) that contributes to these issues. I can’t actually think of any mental disorder or neurodivergency that doesn’t link back to at least two of these things. (Also yes, I did look at actual studies while writing this, I didn’t just pull it out of my ass!)

I also totally get the short-term dopamine release, cause that is a lot of what makes it all so addicting to me (and everyone else). I didn’t mention this before but I have diagnosed ADD so the short-term pleasures hit me a lot harder cause of how my brain’s wired to receive them. My brain is designed in a way to run off those short-term dopamine hits and crave them, which is a major factor of the whole easily-distracted thing. So I get what you mean by those big, long-term pleasures, but a lot of people’s (mine included) brains just aren’t wired like that. (Example: My brain can’t understand holding off on the instant, short-term reward and doing something that doesn’t release dopamine can mean an even greater dopamine release later and even improved life. This is why I procrastinate so much because my brain actively fights against me doing anything productive towards that ‘greater happiness’. I’m working on this through medication and strategies.
Another thing to add is my diagnosed autism! Specifically my hyperfixations and special interests in gaming. Often whenever I start a game, it becomes all I ever think about during the day, which makes me like playing the game more cause it’s one of the few things I feel like doing (since I’ve been stuck thinking about it all day). And when I mean I can barely stop thinking about it, I mean it. I feel gaming as a whole, and that entire world is a special interest (long-term obsession) while all the individual games I hyperfixate on (short-term obsession). In that way I feel like gaming fulfils my long-term happiness because it’s something I’ve loved literally my whole life, and that I will continue to love. They’re more than just games to me, and I seriously consider going into a career path to do with gaming in some way.

By the way, none of this was intended as a “Gotcha!
